title: Flowstate — runs, steps, latency
description: Runs, steps and latency from the metrics Flowstate already emits: otelconnect's RPC instruments on the control plane, and the Temporal SDK's own instruments on the worker. Nothing here is a metric written for a dashboard — if a panel is empty, the interesting question is which pipeline is quiet.

panels.title: Runs started
panels.description: Every `flow run` is one Run RPC, so the control plane can count runs without the engine having to publish a counter for it.

panels.title: RPC latency, p95
panels.description: otelconnect records rpc.server.duration in milliseconds; the collector's Prometheus exporter appends the unit, which is why the series is named _milliseconds.

panels.title: Runs and steps (Temporal SDK, from the worker)
Workflows completed / failed
panels.description: The Temporal SDK's counters arrive as up-down counters, so the Prometheus exporter writes them as gauges — no _total suffix, and rate() is not meaningful. The value is cumulative since the worker started.

panels.title: Run duration, end to end
panels.description: temporal_workflow_endtoend_latency, a histogram in seconds: start to close, including every durable wait — a workflow that sleeps for a day is a day long here, and that is correct rather than a bug.

panels.title: Step execution latency (activities), p95
panels.description: A Flowstate step that does work is a Temporal activity, so this is per-step latency by activity type.

panels.title: Worker task slots available
panels.description: The number that says whether the worker is the bottleneck. Flat at the maximum means idle; near zero means work is queueing behind this worker rather than behind the engine.

panels.title: Everything the SDK is actually emitting
panels.description: Not decoration. Metric names travel through the SDK, the OTLP exporter and the Prometheus exporter, each of which may add a unit or a suffix — so when a panel above is empty, this is where you find out whether the number is missing or merely spelled differently.

panels.title: Workflow task schedule-to-start latency, p95
panels.description: docs/DEPLOYMENT.md's slot-exhaustion runbook says to watch this beside worker task slots — a worker whose slots are full still shows healthy CPU, but a workflow task waiting longer to be picked up is queueing behind this worker rather than behind the engine. Was on the wire and undashboarded before #917; this is the other half of "watch both".

panels.title: Pollers, by type
panels.description: The other capacity signal #526's residue comment claimed was un-instrumented — it was emitted, just not viewed. A poller count sitting at zero for a type this worker should be polling is the same worker-saturation question the slots panel answers, from the queue's side rather than the process's.

panels.title: Run lifecycle (flowstate.run.*, from the driver that observed each run)
Runs started
panels.description: flowstate.run.starts, recorded once per run regardless of how many Continue-As-New segments it takes — never once per segment. Locally at RunWithInputs; durably at engine.Run, through Temporal's replay-safe metrics handler so a replay cannot inflate the count. Compare against the "Runs started" stat above (the Run RPC count): a gap between the two is a run that started some other way — a webhook, a signal that created one — the RPC counter cannot see.

panels.title: Run outcomes, by workflow
panels.description: flowstate.run.executions — the run's own success/failure rate #917 filed for (docs/DEPLOYMENT.md previously recorded no counter existed and asked for this gap to be filed). A Continue-As-New segment boundary is not a completion and is never counted here; only a run's true terminal outcome is.

panels.title: Run duration, p95 (flowstate.run.duration)
panels.description: Start to terminal outcome, by workflow. Durably this is the segment that ends the run, not the sum of every Continue-As-New segment a long workload took — see metricschema.InstrumentRunDuration's doc for why that is the honest answer rather than a plumbed-through timestamp.

panels.title: Server, worker and steps (over OTLP)
panels.description: Log records shipped over OTLP, not lines tailed out of a file — so no query-time parsing, and attributes arrive as attributes. A `log:` step's record carries the trace and span ids of the step it ran in, which is what makes the TraceID field link straight to Tempo. The services' own start-up and shutdown lines are emitted outside any span and carry no trace id; find those by service and time.
